title: Formal glueing: Can is an equivalence of R-modules with glueing data
statement:
Let $\varphi:R\to S$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings, $f_1,\dots,f_t\in R$, and let $\mathrm{Glue}=\mathrm{Glue}(R\to S,f_1,\dots,f_t)$ be the category of glueing data, with the canonical maps $c^P_f:(P\otimes_RS)_f\to P_f\otimes_RS$ and $\sigma^P_{f,g}:(P_f)_g\to(P_g)_f$ and the localizations $P_f$, $h_f$ of [def-weil-pbc-formal-glueing-data]. For an $R$-module $M$ put $\mathrm{Can}(M)=(M\otimes_RS,(M_{f_i})_i,(c^M_{f_i})_i,(\sigma^M_{f_i,f_j})_{i,j})$, and for an $R$-linear map $u:M\to N$ put $\mathrm{Can}(u)=(u\otimes_RS,(u_{f_i})_i)$ [def-weil-module-base-change], [def-weil-pbc-module-localization-away].
(1) For every $R$-module $P$ and $f,g\in R$ the maps $c^P_f$ and $\sigma^P_{f,g}$ are isomorphisms; $\mathrm{Can}(M)$ is an object of $\mathrm{Glue}$, $\mathrm{Can}(u)$ is a morphism $\mathrm{Can}(M)\to\mathrm{Can}(N)$, and $\mathrm{Can}:\mathrm{Mod}_R\to\mathrm{Glue}$ is a functor.
(2) Assume moreover that $\varphi$ is flat [def-weil-pbc-flat-ring-map] and that, for the ideal $I=(f_1,\dots,f_t)$, the induced map $R/I\to S/IS$ is an isomorphism. Then $\mathrm{Can}$ is an equivalence of categories: it is fully faithful (for $R$-modules $M,N$, every morphism $\mathrm{Can}(M)\to\mathrm{Can}(N)$ in $\mathrm{Glue}$ equals $\mathrm{Can}(u)$ for exactly one $R$-linear $u:M\to N$) and essentially surjective (every object of $\mathrm{Glue}$ is isomorphic in $\mathrm{Glue}$ to $\mathrm{Can}(M)$ for some $R$-module $M$).

source.place: More on Algebra, Proposition 05ER (proposition-equivalence, line 24813) and its proof (via Lemmas 05EK, 05EP, 05EQ, 05EI); part (1) is the definition of the functor Can in Remark 05EL (remark-glueing-data, line 24641), where c and sigma are called the canonical isomorphisms can_i, can_ij. Stacks states (2) as: Can and H^0 are quasi-inverse equivalences; only the equivalence property of Can is stated here

proof.text: (Part (1): $c$, $\sigma$ and the object $\mathrm{Can}(M)$.) For every $R$-module $P$ and $f,g\in R$, $\sigma^P_{f,g}$ is an isomorphism with inverse $\sigma^P_{g,f}$, given by $(p/f^a)/g^b\mapsto(p/g^b)/f^a$, and $c^P_f$ is an $S$-linear isomorphism given by $(p\otimes s)/f^e\mapsto(p/f^e)\otimes s$ [lem-weil-pbc-formal-glueing-canonical-maps] (2), (3). Let $M$ be an $R$-module. $M\otimes_RS$ is an $S$-module [def-weil-module-base-change] and $M_{f_i}$ an $R_{f_i}$-module [def-weil-pbc-module-localization-away], so $\mathrm{Can}(M)=(M\otimes_RS,(M_{f_i}),(c^M_{f_i}),(\sigma^M_{f_i,f_j}))$ has the data required in [def-weil-pbc-formal-glueing-data]. Condition (a) for it reads $(\sigma^M_{f_i,f_j}\otimes_RS)\circ c^{M_{f_i}}_{f_j}\circ(c^M_{f_i})_{f_j}=c^{M_{f_j}}_{f_i}\circ(c^M_{f_j})_{f_i}\circ\sigma^{M\otimes S}_{f_i,f_j}$. By the formulas just quoted and the formula $h_f(x/f^e)=h(x)/f^e$ for the localization of a map [def-weil-pbc-module-localization], both sides send $((m\otimes s)/f_i^a)/f_j^b$ to $((m/f_j^b)/f_i^a)\otimes s$: the left side via $((m/f_i^a)\otimes s)/f_j^b$ and $((m/f_i^a)/f_j^b)\otimes s$, the right side via $((m\otimes s)/f_j^b)/f_i^a$ and $((m/f_j^b)\otimes s)/f_i^a$. Every element of $((M\otimes_RS)_{f_i})_{f_j}$ is a finite sum of such elements ($x/f^e$ with $x$ a sum of pure tensors, and $(\sum x_k)/f^e=\sum x_k/f^e$), and both sides are additive, so (a) holds. Condition (b) reads $(\sigma^M_{f_j,f_k})_{f_i}\circ\sigma^{M_{f_j}}_{f_i,f_k}\circ(\sigma^M_{f_i,f_j})_{f_k}=\sigma^{M_{f_k}}_{f_i,f_j}\circ(\sigma^M_{f_i,f_k})_{f_j}\circ\sigma^{M_{f_i}}_{f_j,f_k}$; every element of $((M_{f_i})_{f_j})_{f_k}$ is $((m/f_i^a)/f_j^b)/f_k^c$, and both sides send it to $((m/f_k^c)/f_j^b)/f_i^a$ (left: via $((m/f_j^b)/f_i^a)/f_k^c$, $((m/f_j^b)/f_k^c)/f_i^a$; right: via $((m/f_i^a)/f_k^c)/f_j^b$, $((m/f_k^c)/f_i^a)/f_j^b$). So $\mathrm{Can}(M)$ is an object of $\mathrm{Glue}$.

source.place: More on Algebra, Remark 05EL (remark-glueing-data, line 24641): the functor Can; the canonical isomorphisms can_i, can_ij

proof.text: (Part (1): $\mathrm{Can}$ on maps; functoriality.) Let $u:M\to N$ be $R$-linear. Then $u\otimes_RS$ is $S$-linear [def-weil-module-base-change] and $u_{f_i}$ is $R$-linear [def-weil-pbc-module-localization]. The two conditions for $\mathrm{Can}(u)=(u\otimes_RS,(u_{f_i}))$ to be a morphism [def-weil-pbc-formal-glueing-data] are $c^N_{f_i}\circ(u\otimes_RS)_{f_i}=(u_{f_i}\otimes_RS)\circ c^M_{f_i}$ and $\sigma^N_{f_i,f_j}\circ(u_{f_i})_{f_j}=(u_{f_j})_{f_i}\circ\sigma^M_{f_i,f_j}$. By the formulas of [lem-weil-pbc-formal-glueing-canonical-maps] both sides of the first send $(m\otimes s)/f_i^e$ to $(u(m)/f_i^e)\otimes s$, and both sides of the second send $(m/f_i^a)/f_j^b$ to $(u(m)/f_j^b)/f_i^a$; these elements generate the sources additively (step 1), so both hold. Since $(v\circ u)\otimes_RS=(v\otimes_RS)\circ(u\otimes_RS)$, $\mathrm{id}\otimes_RS=\mathrm{id}$ [def-weil-module-base-change], $(v\circ u)_f=v_f\circ u_f$ and $(\mathrm{id})_f=\mathrm{id}$ [lem-weil-pbc-formal-glueing-canonical-maps] (1), and composition and identities in $\mathrm{Glue}$ are componentwise [def-weil-pbc-formal-glueing-data], $\mathrm{Can}$ is a functor $\mathrm{Mod}_R\to\mathrm{Glue}$. This proves (1). For later use: for an $R$-linear $u$, $\mathrm{Can}(u)$ being a morphism is the naturality $c^N_{f}\circ(u\otimes_RS)_{f}=(u_{f}\otimes_RS)\circ c^M_{f}$, $\sigma^N_{f,g}\circ(u_{f})_{g}=(u_{g})_{f}\circ\sigma^M_{f,g}$.

source.place: More on Algebra, Remark 05EL (remark-glueing-data, line 24641): the functor Can

proof.text: (Part (2): from now on $\varphi$ is flat and $R/I\to S/IS$ is an isomorphism. The complex.) For an $R$-module $N$ let $\alpha_N:N\to(N\otimes_RS)\times\prod_iN_{f_i}$, $n\mapsto(n\otimes1,(n/1)_i)$, and $\beta_N$ be the maps of [lem-weil-pbc-formal-glueing-complex-exact], where $(N\otimes_RS)_{f_i}$ is identified with $N_{f_i}\otimes_RS$ by $c^N_{f_i}$ (the identification of that statement is $(x\otimes s)/f_i^e\leftrightarrow(x/f_i^e)\otimes s$, which is $c^N_{f_i}$ by [lem-weil-pbc-formal-glueing-canonical-maps] (3)). By [lem-weil-pbc-formal-glueing-complex-exact], $\alpha_N$ is injective and $\operatorname{Ker}\beta_N=\operatorname{Im}\alpha_N$. Concretely, a pair $(n',(n_i)_i)$ lies in $\operatorname{Ker}\beta_N$ iff (i) $c^N_{f_i}(n'/1)=n_i\otimes1$ for all $i$ and (ii) $n_i$ and $n_j$ have the same image in $N_{f_if_j}$ under the canonical maps $N_{f_i}\to N_{f_if_j}$, $x/f_i^e\mapsto f_j^ex/(f_if_j)^e$, and $N_{f_j}\to N_{f_if_j}$ [def-weil-pbc-module-localization-away], for all $i,j$.

proof.text: (Part (2): a lemma on iterated localizations.) Let $N$ be an $R$-module, $f,g\in R$, $x,y\in N$, $a,b\ge0$, and suppose $\sigma^N_{f,g}((x/f^a)/1)=(y/g^b)/1$ in $(N_g)_f$. Then $x/f^a$ and $y/g^b$ have the same image in $N_{fg}$. Indeed $\sigma^N_{f,g}((x/f^a)/1)=(x/1)/f^a$ (step 1), so $(x/1)/f^a=(y/g^b)/1$ in $(N_g)_f$: there is $c\ge0$ with $f^c\big(x/1-f^a\cdot y/g^b\big)=0$ in $N_g$, i.e. $(f^cg^bx-f^{c+a}y)/g^b=0$, so there is $d\ge0$ with $g^d(f^cg^bx-f^{a+c}y)=0$ in $N$ [def-weil-pbc-module-localization-away]. The images of $x/f^a$ and $y/g^b$ in $N_{fg}$ are $g^ax/(fg)^a$ and $f^by/(fg)^b$ (canonical maps of [def-weil-pbc-module-localization-away]); their difference is $z/(fg)^{a+b}$ with $z=f^bg^{a+b}x-f^{a+b}g^ay=f^bg^a(g^bx-f^ay)$, and $(fg)^{c+d}z=f^{b+d}g^{a+c}\cdot g^d(f^cg^bx-f^{a+c}y)=0$. Hence the difference is $0$ in $N_{fg}$.

proof.text: (Part (2): $\mathrm{Can}$ is faithful.) Let $u,v:M\to N$ be $R$-linear with $\mathrm{Can}(u)=\mathrm{Can}(v)$, i.e. $u\otimes_RS=v\otimes_RS$ and $u_{f_i}=v_{f_i}$ for all $i$. For $m\in M$, $\alpha_N(u(m))=(u(m)\otimes1,(u(m)/1)_i)=((u\otimes_RS)(m\otimes1),(u_{f_i}(m/1))_i)=\alpha_N(v(m))$, so $u(m)=v(m)$ by injectivity of $\alpha_N$ (step 3).

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma 05EM (lemma-H0-inverse, line 24729), a reformulation of Lemma 05EK (lemma-recover-module-from-glueing-data, line 24579)

proof.text: (Part (2): $\mathrm{Can}$ is full.) Let $(u',(u_i)_i):\mathrm{Can}(M)\to\mathrm{Can}(N)$ be a morphism of $\mathrm{Glue}$ [def-weil-pbc-formal-glueing-data]: $u'$ is $S$-linear, the $u_i:M_{f_i}\to N_{f_i}$ are $R$-linear, $c^N_{f_i}\circ u'_{f_i}=(u_i\otimes_RS)\circ c^M_{f_i}$ and $\sigma^N_{f_i,f_j}\circ(u_i)_{f_j}=(u_j)_{f_i}\circ\sigma^M_{f_i,f_j}$. Let $m\in M$, $n'=u'(m\otimes1)$, $n_i=u_i(m/1)$. Applying the first relation to $(m\otimes1)/1$ gives $c^N_{f_i}(n'/1)=(u_i\otimes_RS)((m/1)\otimes1)=n_i\otimes1$ (formula for $c$, step 1), which is (i) of step 3. Applying the second to $(m/1)/1$ gives $\sigma^N_{f_i,f_j}(n_i/1)=(u_j)_{f_i}((m/1)/1)=n_j/1$; writing $n_i=x/f_i^a$, $n_j=y/f_j^b$, step 4 shows that $n_i$ and $n_j$ have the same image in $N_{f_if_j}$, which is (ii). So $(n',(n_i))\in\operatorname{Ker}\beta_N=\operatorname{Im}\alpha_N$, and by injectivity of $\alpha_N$ there is exactly one $u(m)\in N$ with $u(m)\otimes1=u'(m\otimes1)$ and $u(m)/1=u_i(m/1)$ for all $i$ (step 3). The map $u$ is $R$-linear: $\alpha_N(u(m_1)+r\,u(m_2))$ and $\alpha_N(u(m_1+rm_2))$ are both $(u'((m_1+rm_2)\otimes1),(u_i((m_1+rm_2)/1))_i)$, as $u'$, $u_i$, $\alpha_N$ are $R$-linear. Now $u\otimes_RS$ and $u'$ are $S$-linear and agree on the elements $m\otimes1$, which generate $M\otimes_RS$ over $S$ [def-weil-module-base-change], so $u\otimes_RS=u'$; and $u_{f_i}$, $u_i$ are $R$-linear maps into $N_{f_i}$, on which $f_i$ acts bijectively [def-weil-pbc-module-localization-away], agreeing on the elements $m/1$, so they agree on $m/f_i^e$ (both send it to the unique $z$ with $f_i^ez=u(m)/1$). Hence $(u',(u_i))=\mathrm{Can}(u)$; with step 5, $\mathrm{Can}$ is fully faithful.

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma 05EM (lemma-H0-inverse, line 24729), a reformulation of Lemma 05EK (lemma-recover-module-from-glueing-data, line 24579) (H^0 o Can = id), used in the first sentence of the proof of 05ER

proof.text: (Part (2): the module $H^0(\mathbf M)$ and the morphism $\Psi$.) Let $\mathbf M=(M',(M_i),(\alpha_i),(\alpha_{ij}))$ be an object of $\mathrm{Glue}$. Let $H=H^0(\mathbf M)\subseteq M'\times\prod_iM_i$ be the $R$-module of the families $(m',(m_i))$ with $\alpha_i(m'/1)=m_i\otimes1$ and $\alpha_{ij}(m_i/1)=m_j/1$ for all $i,j$, with projections $p':H\to M'$ and $p_i:H\to M_i$ (Remark 05EL). By [lem-weil-pbc-formal-glueing-H0-localization] there is for each $i$ a unique $R$-linear $\Psi_i:H_{f_i}\to M_i$ with $\Psi_i(h/1)=p_i(h)$, and it is bijective; as $f_i$ acts bijectively on $M_i$, $\Psi_i(h/f_i^e)=f_i^{-e}p_i(h)$. Let $\Psi':H\otimes_RS\to M'$ be the $S$-linear map with $\Psi'(h\otimes s)=s\,p'(h)$ (well defined since $(h,s)\mapsto s\,p'(h)$ is $R$-bilinear [def-weil-module-base-change]). Then $\Psi=(\Psi',(\Psi_i)_i):\mathrm{Can}(H)\to\mathbf M$ is a morphism of $\mathrm{Glue}$ [def-weil-pbc-formal-glueing-data]: (i) $\alpha_i\circ\Psi'_{f_i}=(\Psi_i\otimes_RS)\circ c^H_{f_i}$, since on $(h\otimes s)/f_i^e$ the left side is $\alpha_i(s\,p'(h)/f_i^e)=s f_i^{-e}\alpha_i(p'(h)/1)=sf_i^{-e}(p_i(h)\otimes1)$ ($\alpha_i$ is $S$-linear and $R$-linear) and the right side is $(\Psi_i\otimes_RS)((h/f_i^e)\otimes s)=f_i^{-e}p_i(h)\otimes s$, the same element; (ii) $\alpha_{ij}\circ(\Psi_i)_{f_j}=(\Psi_j)_{f_i}\circ\sigma^H_{f_i,f_j}$, since on $(h/f_i^a)/f_j^b$ the left side is $\alpha_{ij}((f_i^{-a}p_i(h))/f_j^b)=f_i^{-a}f_j^{-b}\alpha_{ij}(p_i(h)/1)=f_i^{-a}f_j^{-b}(p_j(h)/1)$ and the right side is $(\Psi_j)_{f_i}((h/f_j^b)/f_i^a)=(f_j^{-b}p_j(h))/f_i^a$, the same element ($\alpha_{ij}$ is $R$-linear between modules on which $f_i,f_j$ act bijectively, so it commutes with their inverses). These elements generate the sources additively (step 1), using the formulas for $c$ and $\sigma$ [lem-weil-pbc-formal-glueing-canonical-maps].

source.place: More on Algebra, Proposition 05ER (proposition-equivalence, line 24813), proof, first paragraph (the natural morphism Psi); H^0 from Remark 05EL (line 24641)

proof.text: (Part (2): $\Psi'$ has $I$-power torsion kernel and cokernel.) By (i) of step 7, $\Psi'_{f_i}=\alpha_i^{-1}\circ(\Psi_i\otimes_RS)\circ c^H_{f_i}$, a composite of isomorphisms ($\alpha_i$ by [def-weil-pbc-formal-glueing-data], $c^H_{f_i}$ by step 1, $\Psi_i\otimes_RS$ with inverse $\Psi_i^{-1}\otimes_RS$ [def-weil-module-base-change]). Let $K=\operatorname{Ker}\Psi'$ and $Q=\operatorname{Coker}\Psi'$, $S$-modules. Localizing the exact sequences of $R$-modules $0\to K\to H\otimes_RS\xrightarrow{\Psi'}M'$ and $H\otimes_RS\xrightarrow{\Psi'}M'\to Q\to0$ at $\{1,f_i,f_i^2,\dots\}$ gives exact sequences [lem-weil-pbc-localization-module-exact] in which $\Psi'_{f_i}$ is bijective, so $K_{f_i}=0$ and $Q_{f_i}=0$. For $x\in K$ (or $Q$), $x/1=0$ in $K_{f_i}$ gives $e_i$ with $f_i^{e_i}x=0$ [def-weil-pbc-module-localization-away]; with $e=e_1+\dots+e_t$ every monomial $f_1^{a_1}\cdots f_t^{a_t}$ with $\sum a_k=e$ has some $a_k\ge e_k$, and these monomials generate $I^e$, so $I^ex=0$. Hence $K$ and $Q$ are $I$-power torsion.

source.place: More on Algebra, Proposition 05ER (proposition-equivalence, line 24813), proof, second paragraph (kernel and cokernel of Psi are of the form (K,0,0,0), (Q,0,0,0))

proof.text: (Part (2): $\Psi'$ is injective.) Let $y\in K$. Then $y\in(H\otimes_RS)[I^\infty]$ (step 8), and since $I=(f_1,\dots,f_t)$ is finitely generated, $\varphi$ is flat and $R/I\to S/IS$ is an isomorphism, there is $h\in H[I^\infty]$ with $h\otimes1=y$ [lem-weil-pbc-torsion-submodule-flat-base-change-iso]. Then $p'(h)=\Psi'(h\otimes1)=0$. If $I^nh=0$ then $f_i^nh=0$, so $h/1=0$ in $H_{f_i}$ [def-weil-pbc-module-localization-away] and $p_i(h)=\Psi_i(h/1)=0$ for every $i$. As $h=(p'(h),(p_i(h))_i)$ in $M'\times\prod_iM_i$, $h=0$ and $y=0$. So $K=0$. (The source argues with $H^0((K,0,0,0))=K$, left exactness of $H^0$ and bijectivity of $H^0(\Psi)$; the computation here is that argument written out.)

source.place: More on Algebra, Proposition 05ER (proposition-equivalence, line 24813), proof, second paragraph (K = 0)

proof.text: (Part (2): the extension.) The $S$-module $Q$ is $I$-power torsion as an $R$-module (step 8), so $\varepsilon:Q\to Q\otimes_RS$, $x\mapsto x\otimes1$, is bijective [lem-weil-pbc-torsion-module-flat-base-change-iso]. It is $S$-linear: the map $\mu:Q\otimes_RS\to Q$, $x\otimes s\mapsto sx$, is well defined and $S$-linear ($(x,s)\mapsto sx$ is $R$-bilinear [def-weil-module-base-change]), and $\mu\circ\varepsilon=\mathrm{id}_Q$, so $\mu=\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $\varepsilon=\mu^{-1}$ is $S$-linear. With $\rho:M'\to Q$ the cokernel map, $\pi=\varepsilon\circ\rho$ gives, by steps 8 and 9, an exact sequence of $S$-modules $0\to H\otimes_RS\xrightarrow{\Psi'}M'\xrightarrow{\pi}Q\otimes_RS\to0$ (this is the source's 'we may think of $Q$ as an $R$-module which is $I$-power torsion so that $Q=Q\otimes_RS$'). By [lem-weil-pbc-torsion-extension-flat-descent] (with $N=H$, $\iota=\Psi'$) there are an $R$-module $E$, an exact sequence $0\to H\xrightarrow{j}E\xrightarrow{q}Q\to0$ of $R$-modules and an $S$-linear isomorphism $\theta:E\otimes_RS\to M'$ with $\theta\circ(j\otimes_RS)=\Psi'$.

source.place: More on Algebra, Proposition 05ER (proposition-equivalence, line 24813), proof, third paragraph (Lemma 05EH, dualizing-lemma-neighbourhood-extensions, gives E)

proof.text: (Part (2): $\mathrm{Can}(E)\cong\mathbf M$; essential surjectivity.) Since $Q$ is $I$-power torsion, $Q_{f_i}=0$ (each $x\in Q$ has $f_i^nx=0$ for some $n$, so $x/f_i^e=0$ [def-weil-pbc-module-localization-away]); localizing $0\to H\to E\to Q\to0$ [lem-weil-pbc-localization-module-exact] shows that $j_{f_i}:H_{f_i}\to E_{f_i}$ is bijective, and then so are $(j_{f_i})_{f_k}$ and $(j\otimes_RS)_{f_i}=(c^E_{f_i})^{-1}\circ(j_{f_i}\otimes_RS)\circ c^H_{f_i}$ (naturality of $c$, step 2). Put $\Phi_i=\Psi_i\circ j_{f_i}^{-1}:E_{f_i}\to M_i$, an $R$-linear bijection (step 7), and $\Phi=(\theta,(\Phi_i)_i)$. $\Phi:\mathrm{Can}(E)\to\mathbf M$ is a morphism [def-weil-pbc-formal-glueing-data]: (i) precomposed with the bijection $(j\otimes_RS)_{f_i}$, $\alpha_i\circ\theta_{f_i}$ becomes $\alpha_i\circ(\theta\circ(j\otimes_RS))_{f_i}=\alpha_i\circ\Psi'_{f_i}=(\Psi_i\otimes_RS)\circ c^H_{f_i}$ (step 7) and $(\Phi_i\otimes_RS)\circ c^E_{f_i}$ becomes $(\Phi_i\otimes_RS)\circ(j_{f_i}\otimes_RS)\circ c^H_{f_i}=(\Psi_i\otimes_RS)\circ c^H_{f_i}$ (step 2 and functoriality of $-\otimes_RS$ [def-weil-module-base-change]), so $\alpha_i\circ\theta_{f_i}=(\Phi_i\otimes_RS)\circ c^E_{f_i}$; (ii) precomposed with the bijection $(j_{f_i})_{f_k}$, $\alpha_{ik}\circ(\Phi_i)_{f_k}$ becomes $\alpha_{ik}\circ(\Psi_i)_{f_k}=(\Psi_k)_{f_i}\circ\sigma^H_{f_i,f_k}$ (step 7) and $(\Phi_k)_{f_i}\circ\sigma^E_{f_i,f_k}$ becomes $(\Phi_k)_{f_i}\circ(j_{f_k})_{f_i}\circ\sigma^H_{f_i,f_k}=(\Psi_k)_{f_i}\circ\sigma^H_{f_i,f_k}$ (step 2; localization respects composition [lem-weil-pbc-formal-glueing-canonical-maps] (1)), so they are equal. All components of $\Phi$ are bijective, and the family of inverses $(\theta^{-1},(\Phi_i^{-1}))$ is a morphism $\mathbf M\to\mathrm{Can}(E)$ (compose the two relations with the inverses on both sides; $(\Phi_i^{-1})_{f_k}=((\Phi_i)_{f_k})^{-1}$ and $\Phi_i^{-1}\otimes_RS=(\Phi_i\otimes_RS)^{-1}$ by functoriality), inverse to $\Phi$ since composition is componentwise. So $\mathbf M\cong\mathrm{Can}(E)$, and $\mathrm{Can}$ is essentially surjective. With step 6, $\mathrm{Can}$ is an equivalence (fully faithful and essentially surjective), which is (2). (A posteriori $Q=0$, as the source remarks; it is not needed.)

lean.statement: theorem exists_canonical_equivalence {R : Type u} {S : Type v} [CommRing R] [CommRing S] (φ : R →+* S) (t : ℕ) (f : Fin t → R) : (∀ (P : ModuleCat.{max u v w} R) (a b : R), Function.Bijective (compare φ a P) ∧ Function.Bijective (swap a b P)) ∧ ∃ Can : ModuleCat.{max u v w} R ⥤ Data.{u, v, max u v w} φ f, (∀ M : ModuleCat.{max u v w} R, (Can.obj M).M' = extend φ M ∧ (∀ i : Fin t, (Can.obj M).M i = ModuleCat.of (Localization.Away (f i)) (LocalizedModule.Away (f i) M)) ∧ (∀ i : Fin t, HEq ((Can.obj M).alpha i).toLinearMap (compare φ (f i) M)) ∧ (∀ i j : Fin t, HEq ((Can.obj M).alpha_overlap i j).toLinearMap (swap (f i) (f j) M))) ∧ (∀ (M N : ModuleCat.{max u v w} R) (h : M ⟶ N), HEq (Can.map h).prime (extendMap φ h.hom) ∧ ∀ i : Fin t, HEq ((Can.map h).chart i) (localMap (f i) h.hom)) ∧ (φ.Flat → Function.Bijective (Ideal.quotientMap ((Ideal.span (Set.range f)).map φ) φ Ideal.le_comap_map) → (∀ M N : ModuleCat.{max u v w} R, Function.Bijective (Can.map : (M ⟶ N) → (Can.obj M ⟶ Can.obj N))) ∧ (∀ X : Data.{u, v, max u v w} φ f, ∃ M : ModuleCat.{max u v w} R, Nonempty (Can.obj M ≅ X)))
lean.note: The existential functor is specified on every object and morphism by equalities of bundled modules and HEq of linear maps, avoiding any choice of unproved data in a definition. The final conditional asserts bijectivity of all Hom maps and essential surjectivity for this same functor.
